title: A Federal Judge Called Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee an Illegal Tax. The White House Is Fighting Back.
excerpt: The ruling could reshape the economics of hiring foreign workers in America. Indian physicians, engineers, and their employers are caught in the legal crossfire.
body:
In September 2025, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation that added a $100,000 fee to every new H-1B visa petition — a move that overnight transformed the economics of hiring skilled foreign workers in the United States. The fee, which came on top of existing charges that typically totalled $2,000 to $5,000, was framed as a penalty to discourage employers from "replacing American workers with lower-paid, lower-skilled labour."

For the roughly 400,000 H-1B holders of Indian origin — who make up over 70% of all H-1B recipients — the proclamation was existential. Hospitals in rural America, staffed heavily by International Medical Graduates from India, warned they would stop sponsoring physicians. Tech companies said they would move roles offshore. Universities said they could no longer afford research assistants.

On June 8, US District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston struck the fee down entirely.

## The ruling

Sorokin's decision, issued in a lawsuit brought by 20 Democratic state attorneys general, concluded that the $100,000 fee was not a lawful penalty but an unconstitutional tax — one that only Congress, not the president, has the power to levy.

"Here, the substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," Sorokin wrote.

He grounded his reasoning in the Supreme Court's landmark February ruling that struck down Trump's sweeping tariff orders. That decision established that the president cannot use broad executive authority to impose what amounts to a revenue-raising measure without congressional authorisation. Sorokin applied the same logic to the H-1B fee.

The ruling was a direct rebuke of an earlier decision by Judge Beryl Howell in Washington, DC, who had upheld the fee in December 2025 in a case brought by the US Chamber of Commerce. But Howell's ruling came before the Supreme Court's tariff precedent, and Sorokin concluded that the new precedent changed the legal calculus entirely.

## The stay — and what it means

The victory, however, was short-lived. The Trump administration immediately appealed, and the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit issued a stay — meaning the $100,000 fee remains in effect while the appeal plays out. For employers filing new H-1B petitions today, nothing has changed on the ground.

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the administration is "confident" the ruling will be reversed. "President Trump has clear legal authority to restrict entry of any class of aliens he determines is not in America's best interests," she said.

## The healthcare front

The strongest opposition to the fee has come not from Silicon Valley but from American hospitals. The American Association of Physicians of Indian Origin, which represents thousands of Indian-origin doctors across the country, called the ruling "a healthcare victory, not a political one."

"This ruling restores fairness and stability to a system that thousands of international physicians depend upon," said AAPI President Dr. Amit Chakrabarty. "Many hospitals would have struggled to absorb such a financial burden. The consequences would have been immediate — fewer physicians, longer wait times, and reduced access to care for communities that already face healthcare disparities."

International Medical Graduates — physicians trained outside the US and Canada — are a cornerstone of American healthcare, particularly in rural and underserved areas. They fill roles that domestic graduates often do not pursue, and a $100,000 fee per petition would have priced many community hospitals out of the sponsorship market entirely.

## The political split

In a rare bipartisan moment, several Republican lawmakers broke ranks with the White House to support the court's ruling. Their focus was not on tech workers — the usual political battleground for H-1B debates — but on the fee's impact on healthcare and education in their districts.

Rural hospitals, community health centres, and university research departments are among the heaviest users of the H-1B program outside the technology sector. For lawmakers representing these communities, the fee was not an abstract immigration policy question but a direct threat to local services.

Trump, for his part, lambasted the judiciary. "These judges are crazy," he told reporters, describing the decision as part of a broader pattern of judicial overreach that his administration intends to challenge aggressively.

## What comes next

The case now sits with the First Circuit Court of Appeals. Legal experts expect a ruling within three to six months, with the possibility that it ultimately reaches the Supreme Court — which has already signalled, through its tariff ruling, that it takes a dim view of unilateral presidential revenue-raising.

In the meantime, the $100,000 fee continues to apply to new petitions. Indian IT services companies, which are the largest sponsors of H-1B visas, have already begun exploring pass-through arrangements in which some or all of the fee is shared with clients.

## What NRIs should know

For Indian professionals currently on H-1B visas, the fee does not apply to extensions or renewals — only to new petitions. Those considering a transfer to a new employer, however, face the full $100,000 cost, which their new sponsor must absorb or pass on.

The EB-1A "extraordinary ability" green card, which does not require employer sponsorship, has seen a surge in interest as Indian tech professionals seek to decouple their immigration status from their employers. Immigration attorneys report that inquiries for EB-1A self-petitions have roughly doubled since the fee took effect.

The deeper question, however, is political: whether the Supreme Court will ultimately allow a president to set what amounts to a six-figure admission charge for skilled immigrants — or whether that power belongs, as Judge Sorokin ruled, exclusively to Congress.
